bib.title: Agent-Level Patterns (Chapter 9, Agentic Architectural Patterns for Building Multi-Agent Systems)

question: Which patterns define the internal architecture of a single autonomous agent, and in what order should an enterprise adopt them?
hypothesis: Agents should be built incrementally, layering memory, RAG, structured reasoning and multimodal input on a single-agent tool-using baseline.
contributions: Agent Maturity Model mapping agent components (Act/tools, Memory, Reason/plan, Sense) to five patterns
Pattern write-ups (Context, Problem, Solution, Consequences, Implementation guidance) with a loan-agent example and mock Python for each

limits: No experiments, benchmarks or measured results; every number is an invented illustration (loan thresholds 680/740, scores 720, amounts $500,000/$600,000/$750,000).
All code simulates the LLM with if/else and mock tools; ReAct-style tool selection, RAG retrieval and critique are not implemented with a real model.
Claims such as RAG 'drastically reduces hallucinations' and 'lost in the middle' research are asserted without citation or numbers.
The rollout phases (Table 9.2) and metrics (Table 9.3) are examples; no targets or thresholds are given.
Fractal Chain-of-Thought and 'Context Aperture' are described briefly with no reference or evidence.
practices: Adopt capabilities progressively along the Maturity Model: Single Agent Baseline, then memory, RAG, structured reasoning, multimodal input (Table 9.1, strategic guide).
Start with a single tool-using agent (function calling, ReAct or FCoT) before multi-agent designs; it is simplest to debug but scales poorly as tools and domain grow (Single Agent Baseline).
For short-term memory start with a sliding window of the last N turns or summarisation; do not feed the whole history into the context window (Memory, guidance and Note).
For long-term memory use RAG over a vector database and store only high-value data (user profiles, key decisions, finalized facts) to avoid noise (Memory guidance).

Invest in the document pipeline (cleaning, chunking), tailor embedding model and vector DB to the domain, and consider agentic RAG with query reformulation and iterative retrieval for complex queries (RAG guidance).

Compose reasoning patterns: persistent instruction anchoring in all complex prompts, CoT for the first pass, and a critique/auditor second prompt for high-stakes decisions (Structured Reasoning guidance).

Start multimodal work with a pipeline of specialised tools (e.g. OCR then LLM) for control and observability; use a native multimodal model for simpler orchestration and holistic understanding (Multimodal guidance).
Roll out in three phases: Phase 1 baseline plus memory on a high-volume low-risk task, Phase 2 RAG, Phase 3 structured reasoning plus multimodal for high-stakes workflows (Table 9.2).

Measure each pattern: task completion/tool-call success rate; session coherence and repeated-question reduction; hallucination rate against a golden dataset; self-correction trigger rate and preliminary vs final error rate; extraction accuracy on visual tasks (Table 9.3).

terms.definition: the simplest form of an agentic system, where a single agent is tasked with handling a complete workflow by accessing a variety of tools
equip each agent with its own memory or state management system, split into short-term (context window, summarisation, sliding window) and long-term (vector DB or key-value store)
poorly managed memory leading the agent to recall outdated or irrelevant information
the indexed knowledge itself becomes stale or outdated, leading to a decay in performance over time
specialized agents that perform query reformulation or iterative retrieval to improve results
key instructions or goals embedded in the prompt using distinct tags (e.g. #OBJECTIVE:) and repeated at the beginning and end of the context to counteract lost in the middle
the agent generates a preliminary response, then runs a critique step evaluating its output against the original instructions and context
zoom through increasingly detailed Context Aperture levels (macro, meso, micro), applying dual maximising and minimising objective functions, self-reflecting and correcting at each loop
Sense, Reason, Plan, Act, Recall (Memory) as the building blocks of an agent's operational loop
